section: 8.3 Price Discrimination and Market Power
text:
8.3 Price Discrimination and Market Power

1. Conceptual Introduction
So far, we have assumed the monopolist charges every customer the exact same price. Yet firms with market power can often earn far higher profits by practicing price discrimination—selling the exact same product to different customers at different prices not justified by cost differences. Successful price discrimination requires three conditions: (1) the firm must possess market power (a downward-sloping demand curve), (2) the firm must be able to segment buyers by willingness to pay (elasticity), and (3) the firm must prevent arbitrage (resale between low-price and high-price buyers).
Economists classify price discrimination into three degrees:

First-Degree (Perfect) Price Discrimination: Charging every individual buyer their exact maximum willingness to pay. Remarkably, output expands all the way to the competitive level (\(Q_C\)) and Deadweight Loss drops to zero—but the monopolist captures \(100\%\) of Total Social Surplus (\(CS = \$0\)).
Second-Degree Price Discrimination: Offering quantity discounts or tiered menus (such as bulk warehouse packs or airline cabin classes) so buyers self-select based on usage.
Third-Degree Price Discrimination: Dividing customers into observable demographic or behavioral groups—charging a higher price to the group with inelastic demand and a lower price to the group with elastic demand (such as student and senior movie discounts).



2. Visual Representation
Figure 3 compares a single-price monopoly against a third-degree price-discriminating firm charging higher prices to inelastic business travelers and lower prices to elastic leisure students.



Figure 3. Third-Degree Price Discrimination. Setting \(MR_i = MC\) in each separated market segment yields a higher price (\(P_{\text{biz}}\)) for buyers with inelastic demand and a discounted price (\(P_{\text{stu}}\)) for price-sensitive buyers with elastic demand.




3. Real-World Application: Software Student Discounts and Airline Saturday-Night Stays
Software companies like Adobe and Microsoft verify .edu email addresses (preventing resale/arbitrage) to offer Creative Cloud and Office suites at steep discounts to college students while charging full corporate rates to businesses—expanding access to students who would otherwise be priced out while increasing total firm profit.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Under third-degree price discrimination, the firm sets \(MR_1 = MC\) in Segment 1 and \(MR_2 = MC\) in Segment 2 independently:
\[
MR_1(Q_1^*) = MC, \qquad MR_2(Q_2^*) = MC
\]
Worked Problem: A campus theater has a constant Marginal Cost of \(MC = \$4\) per ticket and separates buyers into two groups with verified IDs:

General Public: \(P_1 = 28 - 2Q_1 \implies MR_1 = 28 - 4Q_1\)
Students: \(P_2 = 16 - Q_2 \implies MR_2 = 16 - 2Q_2\)

Calculate the profit-maximizing price and ticket quantity for each group.
Step-by-Step Breakdown:

General Public Segment (\(MR_1 = MC\)):

\[
28 - 4Q_1 = 4 \implies 4Q_1 = 24 \implies Q_1^* = \mathbf{6\text{ tickets}}, \qquad P_1^* = 28 - 2(6) = \mathbf{\$16}
\]

Student Segment (\(MR_2 = MC\)):

\[
16 - 2Q_2 = 4 \implies 2Q_2 = 12 \implies Q_2^* = \mathbf{6\text{ tickets}}, \qquad P_2^* = 16 - 6 = \mathbf{\$10}
\]
Conclusion: The theater charges \(\$16\) to the general public and \(\$10\) to students, maximizing profit across both segments.






NoteOptional Advanced Section: The Lerner Index of Market Power



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: Using \(MR = P\left(1 - \frac{1}{|\varepsilon_d|}\right)\) and setting \(MR = MC\) yields the Lerner Index (\(L\)), which measures percentage markup power as the inverse of demand elasticity:
\[
L = \frac{P - MC}{P} = \frac{1}{|\varepsilon_d|}
\]
In perfect competition (\(|\varepsilon_d| \to \infty\)), \(L = 0\) and \(P = MC\). As demand becomes less elastic, monopoly markup power \(L\) increases.

title: 9  Chapter 9: Monopolistic Competition, Oligopoly, and Game Theory
text:
1. Conceptual Introduction
Most everyday consumer markets—coffee shops, hair salons, casual restaurants, fitness studios, and clothing boutiques—do not fit neatly into either perfect competition or pure monopoly. Instead, they operate under monopolistic competition, a hybrid market structure combining three defining traits: (1) many competing sellers, (2) differentiated products (each seller offers a distinct flavor, location, brand aesthetic, or customer experience), and (3) free entry and exit in the long run.
Because its product is distinct from rivals, each monopolistically competitive firm enjoys a small degree of brand loyalty and faces a downward-sloping demand curve. Just like a monopolist, the firm maximizes short-run profit by producing where Marginal Revenue equals Marginal Cost (\(MR = MC\)) and pricing on its demand curve (\(P > MC\)). However, because there are zero barriers to entry, positive short-run economic profits attract new competitors into the neighborhood—stealing customers and shifting each incumbent firm’s demand curve inward until economic profits are driven to zero.
In long-run equilibrium, the firm’s downward-sloping demand curve becomes tangent to its Average Total Cost (\(ATC\)) curve, enforcing zero economic profit (\(P = ATC\)). Yet unlike perfect competition, this tangency occurs strictly to the left of minimum \(ATC\), creating two permanent structural features: a markup over marginal cost (\(P > MC\)) and excess capacity (\(q_{\text{LR}} < q_{\text{efficient scale}}\)), which represents the cost society pays for product variety.


2. Visual Representation
Figure 1 illustrates the long-run zero-profit equilibrium of a monopolistically competitive firm, highlighting the tangency between demand and \(ATC\) and the resulting excess capacity gap.



Figure 1. Long-Run Equilibrium under Monopolistic Competition. Free entry shifts demand until it is tangent to \(ATC\) at \(q_{\text{LR}}\), yielding zero economic profit (\(P_{\text{LR}} = ATC\)). Because \(q_{\text{LR}} < q_{\text{eff}}\), the firm operates with excess capacity and charges a markup above \(MC\).




3. Real-World Application: Neighborhood Coffee Shops and Retail Differentiation
Walk down any busy commercial avenue and you will see independent cafés every two blocks—one roasting single-origin pour-overs, another offering oat-milk matcha and study booths, and a third specializing in quick drive-thru espresso. None earns monopoly-level economic profits for long because new cafés open whenever neighborhood rents permit, yet each operates below its physical kitchen capacity during mid-afternoon lulls so consumers can enjoy variety and convenience.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
In long-run monopolistic competition, two simultaneous conditions hold at output \(q_{\text{LR}}\):
\[
MR(q_{\text{LR}}) = MC(q_{\text{LR}}) \quad \text{(Profit Maximization)}, \qquad P(q_{\text{LR}}) = ATC(q_{\text{LR}}) \quad \text{(Zero Economic Profit)}
\]
Worked Problem: A boutique fitness studio in a monopolistically competitive neighborhood faces a long-run inverse demand curve \(P = 50 - 2q\) (where \(P\) is class price in dollars and \(q\) is daily clients) and corresponding Marginal Revenue \(MR = 50 - 4q\). Its Marginal Cost is constant at \(MC = \$10\) per client, and its Average Total Cost is \(ATC = \frac{200}{q} + 10\).

Find the studio’s profit-maximizing client volume \(q_{\text{LR}}\) and class price \(P_{\text{LR}}\).
Verify that the studio earns zero economic profit in the long run.
Calculate the firm’s markup over marginal cost (\(P_{\text{LR}} - MC\)).

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Set \(MR = MC\) to Solve for \(q_{\text{LR}}\) and \(P_{\text{LR}}\):

\[
50 - 4q_{\text{LR}} = 10 \implies 4q_{\text{LR}} = 40 \implies q_{\text{LR}} = \mathbf{10\text{ clients per day}}
\]
Substitute \(q_{\text{LR}} = 10\) into the inverse demand curve:
\[
P_{\text{LR}} = 50 - 2(10) = \mathbf{\$30\text{ per class}}
\]

Check Long-Run Economic Profit (\(\pi\)): Compute \(ATC\) at \(q_{\text{LR}} = 10\):

\[
ATC(10) = \frac{200}{10} + 10 = 20 + 10 = \$30\text{ per class}
\]
Since \(P_{\text{LR}}\ (\$30) = ATC\ (\$30)\), economic profit is:
\[
\pi = (\$30 - \$30) \times 10 = \mathbf{\$0}
\]

Compute the Markup over Marginal Cost:

\[
\text{Markup} = P_{\text{LR}} - MC = \$30 - \$10 = \mathbf{\$20\text{ per class}}
\]
Conclusion: The studio breaks even in economic terms (\(\pi = \$0\)) while maintaining a \(\$20\) markup above marginal cost due to product differentiation.

title: 9  Chapter 9: Monopolistic Competition, Oligopoly, and Game Theory
section: 9.2 Oligopoly, Cartels, and Strategic Interdependence
text:
9.2 Oligopoly, Cartels, and Strategic Interdependence

1. Conceptual Introduction
When an industry is dominated by just a handful of large firms—such as commercial aircraft manufacturing (Boeing and Airbus), wireless telecom carriers, or major airlines—the market is an oligopoly. Unlike price-taking farmers or small cafés, oligopolists are acutely aware of one another: every pricing decision, advertising campaign, or product launch by one firm directly affects its rivals’ sales and triggers counter-moves. Economists call this mutual awareness strategic interdependence.
Because oligopolists control the bulk of market supply, they face a powerful temptation to collude—forming a formal or informal cartel to restrict industry output and hold prices up near the monopoly level so they can split monopoly profits. However, cartels suffer from an inherent internal instability. Once a cartel sets a high price above marginal cost (\(P > MC\)), each individual member realizes it can secretly undercut the agreed price slightly, steal its rivals’ customers, and boost its own profit—until all members cheat and prices collapse back toward competitive levels.
Economists measure industry concentration using two standard tools: the Four-Firm Concentration Ratio (\(CR_4\)), which sums the market shares of the four largest firms, and the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (\(HHI\)), which sums the squared market shares of all firms in the market (\(HHI = \sum_{i=1}^N s_i^2\)). Antitrust regulators at the Department of Justice and FTC scrutinize mergers that sharply increase the \(HHI\).


2. Visual Representation
Figure 2 contrasts market outcomes along a quantity-price continuum, showing how an oligopoly settles strictly between the collusive monopoly benchmark (\(Q_M, P_M\)) and the competitive benchmark (\(Q_C, P_C\)).



Figure 2. The Oligopoly Output-Price Spectrum. When oligopolists fail to sustain a cartel, non-cooperative competition expands industry output beyond \(Q_{\text{cartel}}\) and lowers price below \(P_{\text{cartel}}\), moving the market closer to the competitive outcome \((Q_C, P_C)\).




3. Real-World Application: OPEC Production Quotas and Cheating Incentives
The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) acts as an international oil cartel, agreeing on production quotas to keep global crude oil prices elevated. Whenever OPEC successfully restricts output and pushes oil prices to \(\$90\) per barrel, individual member countries face an immediate temptation to quietly pump above their assigned quota—selling extra barrels at \(\$90\) while extraction costs are only \(\$20\)—frequently triggering price wars and quota breakdowns.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
The Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (\(HHI\)) squares each firm’s percentage market share \(s_i\) (from \(0\) to \(100\)):
\[
HHI = s_1^2 + s_2^2 + \dots + s_N^2
\]
Worked Problem: A regional wireless internet market is served by four providers with market shares of \(40\%\), \(30\%\), \(20\%\), and \(10\%\).

Compute the Four-Firm Concentration Ratio (\(CR_4\)) and the baseline \(HHI\).
Compute the new post-merger \(HHI\) if the two smallest providers (\(20\%\) and \(10\%\)) merge into a single \(30\%\) firm.

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Calculate Baseline \(CR_4\) and \(HHI\):

\[
CR_4 = 40\% + 30\% + 20\% + 10\% = \mathbf{100\%}
\]
\[
HHI_{\text{pre}} = 40^2 + 30^2 + 20^2 + 10^2 = 1{,}600 + 900 + 400 + 100 = \mathbf{3{,}000}
\]

Calculate Post-Merger \(HHI\) (Shares: \(40\%\), \(30\%\), \(30\%\)):

\[
HHI_{\text{post}} = 40^2 + 30^2 + 30^2 = 1{,}600 + 900 + 900 = \mathbf{3{,}400}
\]
Conclusion: The merger raises the \(HHI\) by \(400\) points (from \(3{,}000\) to \(3{,}400\)), flagging a highly concentrated oligopoly for regulatory review.

9.3 Game Theory, Dominant Strategies, and Nash Equilibrium

1. Conceptual Introduction
Because oligopolists cannot make decisions in a vacuum, economists analyze their behavior using game theory—the mathematical study of strategic decision-making when each player’s payoff depends on the actions of other players. Every strategic game consists of three building blocks: (1) the players, (2) the strategies available to each player, and (3) the payoffs resulting from every combination of choices.
To predict how rational rivals will behave without binding contracts, economists look for two key concepts:

Dominant Strategy: A strategy that yields a strictly higher payoff for a player no matter what strategy the rival chooses. If a player has a dominant strategy, they will always play it.
Nash Equilibrium: An outcome in which every player is choosing their best response given what the other players are doing. At a Nash equilibrium, no player can improve their own payoff by unilaterally changing their strategy.

The most famous game in economics is the Prisoner’s Dilemma. In this game, both firms could earn higher joint profits by cooperating (e.g., keeping prices high or limiting advertising), yet each firm’s individual dominant strategy is to defect (slash prices or flood the market with ads). As a result, rational self-interest locks both firms into a non-cooperative Nash equilibrium where both earn lower profits!


2. Visual Representation
Figure 3 presents a \(2 \times 2\) payoff matrix for two competing streaming platforms deciding between keeping subscription prices high (\(\$18\)) or discounting to capture subscribers (\(\$12\)).






NoteClear It Up: Why Prisoners’ Dilemmas Are Good News for Consumers



In a business pricing game, failure to cooperate traps rival firms in a low-price Nash equilibrium—which hurts the firms’ combined profits, yet benefits consumers through lower prices and higher consumer surplus! Antitrust laws exist specifically to prevent oligopolists from escaping their Prisoner’s Dilemma through illegal price-fixing agreements.





Figure 3. A \(2 \times 2\) Pricing Prisoner’s Dilemma (Annual Profits in Millions). Underlined payoffs show each firm’s best response. Both firms have a dominant strategy to Discount (\(\$12\)), landing in the bottom-right Nash equilibrium (\(\$35\text{M}, \$35\text{M}\)) rather than the cooperative outcome (\(\$50\text{M}, \$50\text{M}\)).




3. Real-World Application: Airline Fare Wars and Repeated Interaction
When two airlines compete on the same nonstop route (such as San Francisco to Los Angeles), matching a competitor’s fare cut within hours via automated pricing software acts as a tit-for-tat enforcement mechanism. Because airlines interact repeatedly day after day rather than playing a one-shot game, the credible threat of immediate retaliation helps stabilize fares without explicit collusion.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
To solve any \(2 \times 2\) simultaneous game for a Nash equilibrium, evaluate each player’s conditional best responses:
\[
\text{Strategy } s_A^* \text{ is a Best Response to } s_B^* \iff \pi_A(s_A^*, s_B^*) \ge \pi_A(s_A, s_B^*) \quad \forall s_A
\]
Worked Problem: Using the payoff matrix in Figure 3, prove mathematically why Discount (\(\$12\)) is a strictly dominant strategy for Firm A and verify that (Discount, Discount) is the unique Nash equilibrium.
Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Check Firm A’s Best Response When Firm B Plays “Price High (\(\$18\))”: Compare Firm A’s profit in the left column:

\[
\pi_A(\text{Discount} \mid \text{B High}) = \$65\text{M} > \pi_A(\text{High} \mid \text{B High}) = \$50\text{M}
\]
Firm A earns \(\$15\text{M}\) more by discounting.

Check Firm A’s Best Response When Firm B Plays “Discount (\(\$12\))”: Compare Firm A’s profit in the right column:

\[
\pi_A(\text{Discount} \mid \text{B Discount}) = \$35\text{M} > \pi_A(\text{High} \mid \text{B Discount}) = \$20\text{M}
\]
Firm A again earns \(\$15\text{M}\) more by discounting.

Confirm Dominant Strategy and Nash Equilibrium: Because Discount yields a higher payoff regardless of Firm B’s choice, Discount is Firm A’s strictly dominant strategy. By symmetry, Discount is also Firm B’s strictly dominant strategy. At (Discount, Discount), neither firm can raise its profit above \(\$35\text{M}\) by switching unilaterally to High (which drops its profit to \(\$20\text{M}\)).

Conclusion: (Discount, Discount) with payoffs \((\$35\text{M}, \$35\text{M})\) is the unique Nash equilibrium, even though both firms would earn \(\$50\text{M}\) each if they could credibly cooperate.






NoteOptional Advanced Section: Cournot Duopoly Best-Response Functions



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: In a continuous quantity-setting Cournot duopoly facing inverse demand \(P = 100 - (q_1 + q_2)\) with constant marginal cost \(MC = 10\), Firm 1 maximizes \(\pi_1 = [100 - q_1 - q_2]q_1 - 10q_1\). Setting \(\frac{\partial \pi_1}{\partial q_1} = 90 - 2q_1 - q_2 = 0\) yields Firm 1’s continuous best-response function:
\[
q_1^*(q_2) = 45 - \frac{1}{2}q_2
\]
By symmetry, \(q_2^*(q_1) = 45 - \frac{1}{2}q_1\). Solving simultaneously gives the Cournot-Nash equilibrium output \(q_1^* = q_2^* = 30\) (total output \(Q = 60\), price \(P = \$40\)), lying strictly between the cartel output (\(Q_M = 45, P_M = \$55\)) and competitive output (\(Q_C = 90, P_C = \$10\)).

title: 10  Chapter 10: Externalities, Public Goods, and Common Resources
text:
1. Conceptual Introduction
In Chapter 4, we showed that competitive markets maximize total social surplus when private buyers and sellers capture all benefits and pay all costs of a transaction (\(MB = MC\)). However, markets fail to allocate resources efficiently whenever production or consumption creates an externality—an uncompensated cost or benefit imposed on a third party outside the market transaction.
Externalities split into two fundamental categories:

Negative Externalities (External Costs): When producing or consuming a good imposes unpriced harm on bystanders—such as industrial air pollution, highway traffic congestion, or late-night noise—the Marginal Social Cost (\(MSC\)) exceeds the firm’s Marginal Private Cost (\(MPC\)) by the Marginal External Cost (\(MEC\)): \(MSC = MPC + MEC\). Because unregulated firms ignore \(MEC\) and produce where \(MB = MPC\), the free market overproduces (\(Q_{\text{market}} > Q_{\text{efficient}}\)), creating a Deadweight Loss triangle on the excess units.
Positive Externalities (External Benefits): When an activity generates unpriced spillover benefits for third parties—such as vaccinations reducing disease transmission, basic scientific research, or home solar installations—the Marginal Social Benefit (\(MSB\)) exceeds Marginal Private Benefit (\(MPB\)) by the Marginal External Benefit (\(MEB\)): \(MSB = MPB + MEB\). Left alone, the market produces where \(MPB = MC\) and underproduces (\(Q_{\text{market}} < Q_{\text{efficient}}\)).



2. Visual Representation
Figure 1 illustrates a negative production externality where \(MSC\) lies above \(MPC\) by the vertical distance \(MEC\), causing unregulated market output \(Q_M\) to exceed the socially efficient output \(Q^*\) and generating an orange Deadweight Loss triangle.



Figure 1. Negative Production Externality. Because firms ignore Marginal External Cost (\(MEC\)), the unregulated market produces \(Q_M = 40\) where \(MB = MPC\) instead of the socially optimal \(Q^* = 35\) where \(MB = MSC\), generating Deadweight Loss on the five overproduced units.




3. Real-World Application: Urban Traffic Congestion and Carbon Emissions
During rush hour on Bay Area bridges and freeways, every additional driver entering the highway slows down thousands of commuters behind them—an unpriced external time cost (\(MEC\)). Similarly, industrial carbon dioxide emissions impose climate damages outside the factory gate, separating measured physical emissions (tracked in St. Louis Fed FRED series EMISSCO2TOTVTTTOUSA) from marginal external dollar damages.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Comparing unregulated equilibrium (\(MB = MPC\)) with social efficiency (\(MB = MSC = MPC + MEC\)):
\[
DWL = \frac{1}{2} \times (Q_M - Q^*) \times MEC(Q_M)
\]
Worked Problem: Using the linear model in Figure 1, suppose inverse marginal benefit is \(MB = 100 - Q\), marginal private cost is \(MPC = 20 + Q\), and marginal external cost is a constant \(MEC = \$10\) per unit. Compute \(Q_M\), \(Q^*\), and Deadweight Loss (\(DWL\)).
Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Find Unregulated Output (\(Q_M\)) Where \(MB = MPC\):

\[
100 - Q_M = 20 + Q_M \implies 2Q_M = 80 \implies Q_M = \mathbf{40\text{ units}}
\]

Construct \(MSC\) and Find Efficient Output (\(Q^*\)) Where \(MB = MSC\):

\[
MSC = MPC + MEC = (20 + Q) + 10 = 30 + Q
\]
Set \(MB = MSC\):
\[
100 - Q^* = 30 + Q^* \implies 2Q^* = 70 \implies Q^* = \mathbf{35\text{ units}}
\]

Compute Deadweight Loss (\(DWL\)) from Overproduction:

\[
DWL = \frac{1}{2} \times (40 - 35) \times \$10 = \frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times \$10 = \mathbf{\$25}
\]
Conclusion: Ignoring the \(\$10\) external damage leads the market to overproduce by \(5\) units and destroys \(\$25\) in social welfare.

10.2 Corrective Policies: Pigouvian Taxes, Subsidies, and Coase Bargaining

1. Conceptual Introduction
How can society restore efficiency when externalities distort market outcomes? Economists evaluate both private bargaining solutions and public policy tools designed to internalize the externality—forcing decision-makers to weigh external costs or benefits inside their own private calculations:

Pigouvian Taxes and Subsidies: Named after economist Arthur Pigou, a Pigouvian tax sets a per-unit tax equal to Marginal External Cost at the efficient quantity (\(t^* = MEC(Q^*)\)), shifting \(MPC\) upward onto \(MSC\) so firms voluntarily choose \(Q^*\). Conversely, a Pigouvian subsidy equal to \(MEB(Q^*)\) corrects positive externalities.
Cap-and-Trade (Tradable Permits): Regulators cap total emissions at \(Q^*\) and allow firms to buy and sell permits—achieving the exact same pollution reduction at the lowest possible abatement cost across firms.
The Coase Theorem: Economist Ronald Coase proved that if property rights are clearly defined and transaction costs are low, private parties can bargain directly to reach the efficient outcome \(Q^*\) without government intervention—regardless of which party initially holds the property right. However, when millions of dispersed residents are affected by urban smog, high transaction costs prevent private bargaining and require public policy.



2. Visual Representation
Figure 2 shows how levying a Pigouvian corrective tax \(t^* = MEC = \$10\) shifts the private supply curve from \(MPC\) onto \(MSC\), eliminating deadweight loss and guiding the market cleanly to \(Q^* = 35\).






NoteClear It Up: Why a Pigouvian Tax Increases Welfare Instead of Causing DWL



In Chapter 4, taxing a distortion-free market created deadweight loss. When a market already suffers from a negative externality, however, a Pigouvian tax eliminates deadweight loss by stopping overproduction where social cost exceeds social benefit (\(MSC > MB\))!





Figure 2. Correcting a Negative Externality with a Pigouvian Tax. Setting \(t^* = MEC = \$10\) shifts private cost from \(MPC\) to \(MSC\), contracting output from \(40\) to \(Q^* = 35\) and raising \(\$350\) in revenue while eliminating deadweight loss.




3. Real-World Application: California’s Cap-and-Trade Program
California enforces a statewide cap on greenhouse gas emissions across power plants, refineries, and industrial facilities while allowing companies to trade emission allowances. Firms that can cut emissions cheaply sell spare permits to firms facing higher abatement costs, achieving the statewide emissions cap at minimum economic cost.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
To restore efficiency, set the corrective tax or subsidy equal to the marginal spillover at \(Q^*\):
\[
t^* = MEC(Q^*), \qquad s^* = MEB(Q^*)
\]
Worked Problem: Suppose community flu vaccinations have private marginal benefit \(MPB = 80 - 2Q\), marginal social benefit \(MSB = 100 - 2Q\), and constant marginal cost \(MC = \$30\) per dose (where \(Q\) is thousands of doses). Compute the unregulated vaccination quantity \(Q_M\), the socially efficient quantity \(Q^*\), and the optimal Pigouvian subsidy \(s^*\) per dose.
Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Find Unregulated Quantity (\(Q_M\)) Where \(MPB = MC\):

\[
80 - 2Q_M = 30 \implies 2Q_M = 50 \implies Q_M = \mathbf{25\text{ thousand doses}}
\]

Find Efficient Quantity (\(Q^*\)) Where \(MSB = MC\):

\[
100 - 2Q^* = 30 \implies 2Q^* = 70 \implies Q^* = \mathbf{35\text{ thousand doses}}
\]

Compute the Optimal Pigouvian Subsidy (\(s^*\)):

\[
s^* = MSB - MPB = (100 - 2Q) - (80 - 2Q) = \mathbf{\$20\text{ per dose}}
\]
Conclusion: A \(\$20\) per-dose subsidy lowers the out-of-pocket price to \(\$10\), expanding vaccinations from \(25{,}000\) to the socially optimal \(35{,}000\) doses.

text:
10.3 Public Goods, Common Resources, and the Free-Rider Problem

1. Conceptual Introduction
Economists classify all goods in society using two physical questions: (1) Is the good excludable (can sellers prevent non-payers from using it)? and (2) Is the good rival in consumption (does one person’s use reduce the amount available for others)?
Crossing these two traits creates a four-quadrant classification matrix:

Private Goods (Excludable & Rival): Coffee, laptops, and sneakers. Private markets supply these efficiently.
Club Goods (Excludable & Non-Rival): Streaming services, toll roads without congestion, and private Wi-Fi.
Public Goods (Non-Excludable & Non-Rival): National defense, municipal storm sirens, and basic scientific knowledge. Because nobody can be excluded once provided, individuals face a temptation to enjoy the benefit without paying—known as the free-rider problem—causing private markets to underprovide public goods unless funded through taxation.
Common Resources (Non-Excludable & Rival): Open-ocean fisheries, clean air, and congested public highways. Because anyone can access the resource for free yet each user depletes what remains for others, individuals overuse common resources—a market failure known as the Tragedy of the Commons.



2. Visual Representation
Figure 3 organizes the four economic categories of goods by excludability and rivalry, and contrasts private horizontal demand summation against public-good vertical willingness-to-pay summation.



Figure 3. The Four Economic Categories of Goods. Non-excludability creates two distinct market failures: underprovision of non-rival Public Goods (free riding) and overexploitation of rival Common Resources (Tragedy of the Commons).




3. Real-World Application: Pacific Salmon Fisheries and Catch Shares
Open-ocean fisheries are classic common resources: every fishing boat captures the full revenue of the fish it hauls in, while ignoring the external depletion cost imposed on future breeding stocks. Regulated Individual Transferable Quotas (ITQs) assign enforceable property rights over sustainable catch limits, preventing fishery collapse.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Because a public good is non-rival (everyone consumes the same quantity \(Q\)), total Marginal Social Benefit (\(MSB\)) sums individual marginal willingness to pay vertically:
\[
MSB(Q) = MB_1(Q) + MB_2(Q) + \dots + MB_N(Q) = MC(Q)
\]
Worked Problem: Two neighboring towns, Oakville and Pinehurst, share a coastal tsunami warning siren network. Oakville’s marginal benefit is \(MB_1 = 50 - Q\), and Pinehurst’s marginal benefit is \(MB_2 = 30 - Q\), where \(Q\) is the number of sirens installed. The marginal cost of installing each siren is \(MC = \$40\).

Determine how many sirens either town would buy acting alone.
Compute the socially optimal number of sirens \(Q^*\) by summing marginal benefits vertically.

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Check Individual Provision (\(MB_i = MC\)):
Oakville alone: \(50 - Q_1 = 40 \implies Q_1 = \mathbf{10\text{ sirens}}\).
Pinehurst alone: \(30 - Q_2 = 40 \implies Q_2 = \mathbf{0\text{ sirens}}\) (since its maximum willingness to pay \(\$30 < \$40\)).
Sum Marginal Benefits Vertically (\(MSB = MB_1 + MB_2\)) and Set Equal to \(MC\):

\[
MSB(Q) = (50 - Q) + (30 - Q) = 80 - 2Q
\]
Set \(MSB = MC\):
\[
80 - 2Q^* = 40 \implies 2Q^* = 40 \implies Q^* = \mathbf{20\text{ sirens}}
\]
Conclusion: Acting independently, the towns install at most \(10\) sirens; pooling their joint valuation yields the socially optimal \(20\) sirens.






NoteOptional Advanced Section: Samuelson Condition for Public Goods



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: For \(N\) consumers with utility functions \(U_i(x_i, G)\) over private good \(x_i\) and non-rival public good \(G\), Pareto efficiency requires the Samuelson Condition: the sum of Marginal Rates of Substitution across all citizens must equal the Marginal Rate of Transformation:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{N} MRS_{G, x}^i = MRT_{G, x}
\]
Unlike private goods (where \(MRS^1 = MRS^2 = MRT\)), public goods sum marginal valuations across the entire population because every citizen consumes the same unit of \(G\) simultaneously.

title: 11  Chapter 11: Consumer Choice Theory: Utility and Indifference Curves
text:
1. Conceptual Introduction
Behind every downward-sloping market demand curve lies millions of individual household decisions. To model how rational consumers allocate limited dollars across competing goods, economists separate what a consumer can afford from what a consumer wants. The boundary of affordability is captured by the budget constraint (or budget line), which plots all combinations of two goods—say, campus meals (\(X\)) and commuter transit passes (\(Y\))—that exhaust a consumer’s fixed monthly income \(I\) at given market prices \(P_x\) and \(P_y\).
Every point on or inside the budget line belongs to the consumer’s affordable budget set (\(P_x X + P_y Y \le I\)), while bundles outside the line are unaffordable. The steepness of the budget line reflects the relative price of the two goods: its slope equals \(-P_x / P_y\), measuring the exact opportunity cost of buying one additional unit of Good \(X\) in terms of forgone units of Good \(Y\).
Changes in income and prices transform the budget line in two geometrically distinct ways:

A Change in Income (\(I\)): Holding prices fixed, higher income shifts the entire budget line outward in parallel (preserving the exact same slope \(-P_x / P_y\)), whereas lower income shifts it inward in parallel.
A Change in One Price (\(P_x\) or \(P_y\)): Holding income and the other price fixed, a drop in \(P_x\) rotates (pivots) the budget line outward along the horizontal \(X\)-axis while keeping the vertical \(Y\)-intercept anchored.



2. Visual Representation
Figure 1 illustrates a baseline budget constraint alongside a parallel outward shift from higher income (left) and an outward pivot from a lower price of Good \(X\) (right).



Figure 1. Shifts and Pivots of the Budget Line. In panel (a), an increase in income at constant prices shifts the budget line outward in parallel. In panel (b), a reduction in the price of \(X\) pivots the line outward around the fixed vertical intercept \(I / P_y\).




3. Real-World Application: Transit Subsidies vs. Unrestricted Cash Stipends
Suppose a university wants to help low-income students commute and eat on campus. Giving students a \(\$60\) unrestricted cash stipend shifts their budget constraint outward in parallel (expanding choices across all goods), whereas subsidizing campus meal plans by \(50\%\) pivots the budget line outward along the meals axis—altering the relative price ratio and incentivizing students to consume more campus meals specifically.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Solving the budget identity \(P_x X + P_y Y = I\) for \(Y\) expresses the budget line in slope-intercept form:
\[
Y = \frac{I}{P_y} - \frac{P_x}{P_y}X
\]
Worked Problem: A student has a monthly entertainment budget of \(I = \$120\) to spend on movie tickets (\(P_x = \$15\) each) and paperback books (\(P_y = \$20\) each).

Find the horizontal intercept, vertical intercept, and slope of the student’s budget line.
Write the budget line equation in slope-intercept form (\(Y\) as a function of \(X\)).
Suppose a student discount lowers movie ticket prices to \(P_x^{\text{new}} = \$10\). Find the new horizontal intercept and slope.

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Compute Baseline Intercepts and Slope:

\[
X_{\max} = \frac{\$120}{\$15} = \mathbf{8\text{ movies}}, \qquad Y_{\max} = \frac{\$120}{\$20} = \mathbf{6\text{ books}}
\]
\[
\text{Slope} = -\frac{P_x}{P_y} = -\frac{15}{20} = \mathbf{-0.75\text{ books per movie}}
\]

Write the Slope-Intercept Equation:

\[
Y = \mathbf{6 - 0.75X}
\]

Recompute After Price Drop to \(P_x^{\text{new}} = \$10\): The vertical intercept stays anchored at \(Y_{\max} = \mathbf{6\text{ books}}\), while the horizontal intercept expands to:

\[
X_{\max}^{\text{new}} = \frac{\$120}{\$10} = \mathbf{12\text{ movies}}, \qquad \text{Slope}^{\text{new}} = -\frac{10}{20} = \mathbf{-0.50\text{ books per movie}}
\]
Conclusion: Lowering movie ticket prices to \(\$10\) rotates the budget line outward along the horizontal axis and reduces the opportunity cost of a movie from \(0.75\) books to \(0.50\) books.

section: 11.2 Preferences, Indifference Curves, and Optimal Tangency
text:
11.2 Preferences, Indifference Curves, and Optimal Tangency

1. Conceptual Introduction
Once the budget line defines what is affordable, consumer preferences determine which affordable bundle yields the highest satisfaction, or utility. Because happiness cannot be measured on an objective thermometer across different people, modern economics treats utility as an ordinal ranking: utility numbers simply rank bundles from least preferred to most preferred.
To map preferences geometrically, economists draw indifference curves—each curve connects all bundles \((X, Y)\) that leave the consumer equally satisfied. Well-behaved indifference curves obey four properties: (1) curves further from the origin represent higher utility (more is preferred to less), (2) indifference curves slope downward, (3) indifference curves never cross, and (4) indifference curves are bowed inward (convex to the origin). Convexity reflects diminishing Marginal Rate of Substitution (\(MRS_{XY}\)): the more meals you already have relative to transit trips, the fewer transit trips you are willing to give up to get one more meal.
To maximize utility subject to their budget, a consumer selects the bundle on the highest reachable indifference curve—occurring at the exact tangency point where the slope of the indifference curve equals the slope of the budget line:
\[
MRS_{XY} = \frac{MU_x}{MU_y} = \frac{P_x}{P_y} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \frac{MU_x}{P_x} = \frac{MU_y}{P_y}
\]
In plain English, the equimarginal principle states that the last dollar spent on Good \(X\) must deliver the exact same marginal utility per dollar as the last dollar spent on Good \(Y\).


2. Visual Representation
Figure 2 shows the consumer’s optimal bundle \(E^*(7.5, 10)\) where indifference curve \(U_2\) is tangent to the budget line, strictly outperforming affordable non-tangent points like \(A\) on lower curve \(U_1\).



Figure 2. Utility Maximization at Tangency. The consumer reaches the highest attainable indifference curve \(U_2\) at bundle \(E^*(7.5, 10)\), where the slope of the indifference curve (\(-MRS_{XY}\)) matches the slope of the budget line (\(-P_x / P_y\)).




3. Real-World Application: Grocery Shopping and the Equimarginal Rule
When shoppers compare \(\$12\) organic berries against \(\$3\) bananas at the grocery store, they instinctively apply \(\frac{MU_{\text{berries}}}{P_{\text{berries}}} = \frac{MU_{\text{bananas}}}{P_{\text{bananas}}}\): berries must feel at least four times as satisfying per carton as bananas to justify taking up four times as much budget space.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
To solve for an interior consumer optimum, combine the tangency condition with the budget equation:
\[
\frac{MU_x}{MU_y} = \frac{P_x}{P_y} \quad \text{and} \quad P_x X + P_y Y = I
\]
Worked Problem: A student allocates \(I = \$60\) per month between meals (\(X\)) priced at \(P_x = \$4\) and transit trips (\(Y\)) priced at \(P_y = \$3\). The student’s utility function is \(U(X, Y) = X \cdot Y\), with marginal utilities \(MU_x = Y\) and \(MU_y = X\). Solve for the utility-maximizing bundle \((X^*, Y^*)\).
Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Apply the Tangency Condition (\(MRS_{XY} = P_x / P_y\)):

\[
\frac{MU_x}{MU_y} = \frac{P_x}{P_y} \implies \frac{Y}{X} = \frac{4}{3} \implies Y = \frac{4}{3}X
\]

Substitute \(Y = \frac{4}{3}X\) into the Budget Constraint (\(4X + 3Y = 60\)):

\[
4X + 3\left(\frac{4}{3}X\right) = 60 \implies 4X + 4X = 60 \implies 8X = 60 \implies X^* = \mathbf{7.5\text{ meals}}
\]

Solve for \(Y^*\) and Verify Total Spending:

\[
Y^* = \frac{4}{3}(7.5) = \mathbf{10\text{ transit trips}}
\]
Check budget exhaustion: \(\$4(7.5) + \$3(10) = \$30 + \$30 = \$60\).
Conclusion: Purchasing \(7.5\) meals and \(10\) transit trips maximizes utility at \(U = 7.5 \times 10 = 75\).

section: 11.3 Income and Substitution Effects of a Price Change
text:
11.3 Income and Substitution Effects of a Price Change

1. Conceptual Introduction
When the price of a good falls—say, laptop prices drop by \(25\%\)—consumers almost always buy more of it. Economists decompose this total change in quantity demanded into two distinct behavioral mechanisms:

The Substitution Effect: Because laptops are now cheaper relative to tablets and smartphones, consumers substitute away from relatively pricier alternatives and buy more laptops, holding real purchasing power constant along the initial indifference curve. The substitution effect always moves in the opposite direction of the price change (\(P_x \downarrow \implies X_{\text{sub}} \uparrow\)).
The Income Effect: A lower laptop price stretches the consumer’s fixed paycheck further, boosting their real purchasing power. For a normal good, higher purchasing power raises quantity demanded further (\(X_{\text{inc}} \uparrow\)), reinforcing the substitution effect. For an inferior good, higher purchasing power reduces quantity demanded (\(X_{\text{inc}} \downarrow\)), partially offsetting the substitution effect.



2. Visual Representation
Figure 3 decomposes a price drop from \(P_{x1}\) to \(P_{x2}\) into the substitution effect (\(E_1 \to E_{\text{comp}}\) along \(U_1\)) and the income effect (\(E_{\text{comp}} \to E_2\) onto higher indifference curve \(U_2\)).






NoteClear It Up: What Is a Giffen Good?



For almost all inferior goods, the negative substitution effect of a price hike still overpowers the positive income effect, keeping the demand curve downward sloping. Only in an extraordinary theoretical case—a Giffen good, where an inferior staple consumes such a huge share of a poor household’s budget that the income effect outweighs the substitution effect—could a price rise ever increase quantity demanded.





Figure 3. Hicksian Decomposition of a Price Decrease. The movement from \(X_1\) to \(X_c\) along \(U_1\) isolates the pure Substitution Effect, while the outward shift from \(X_c\) to \(X_2\) onto \(U_2\) captures the Income Effect for a normal good.




3. Real-World Application: Gasoline Price Spikes and Commuter Behavior
When retail gasoline jumps from \(\$3.50\) to \(\$5.50\) per gallon, commuters respond through both channels: the substitution effect pushes drivers to carpool, take public transit, or combine errands, while the income effect leaves households with less discretionary money left over for dining out or weekend travel.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Total quantity change equals the sum of the substitution and income effects:
\[
\Delta X_{\text{total}} = X_2 - X_1 = \underbrace{(X_c - X_1)}_{\text{Substitution Effect}} + \underbrace{(X_2 - X_c)}_{\text{Income Effect}}
\]
Worked Problem: Continuing our Cobb-Douglas student (\(U = XY\), \(I = \$60\), \(P_y = \$3\)), initially \(P_{x1} = \$4\) and the student buys \(X_1 = 7.5\) meals and \(Y_1 = 10\) trips (\(U_1 = 75\)). Suppose a campus dining discount lowers meal prices to \(P_{x2} = \$2\).

Find the new optimal bundle \((X_2, Y_2)\) and total change in meals \(\Delta X_{\text{total}}\).
Given that the compensated meal quantity keeping \(U_1 = 75\) at the new price ratio is \(X_c \approx 10.6\) meals, separate \(\Delta X_{\text{total}}\) into the substitution effect and the income effect.

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Solve for New Optimal Bundle (\(X_2, Y_2\)) at \(P_{x2} = \$2\): Tangency requires \(\frac{Y}{X} = \frac{2}{3} \implies Y = \frac{2}{3}X\). Plug into \(2X + 3Y = 60\):

\[
2X + 3\left(\frac{2}{3}X\right) = 60 \implies 4X = 60 \implies X_2 = \mathbf{15\text{ meals}}, \qquad Y_2 = \mathbf{10\text{ trips}}
\]
Total change in meals: \(\Delta X_{\text{total}} = 15 - 7.5 = \mathbf{+7.5\text{ meals}}\).

Decompose into Substitution and Income Effects:

\[
\text{Substitution Effect} = X_c - X_1 = 10.6 - 7.5 = \mathbf{+3.1\text{ meals}}
\]
\[
\text{Income Effect} = X_2 - X_c = 15.0 - 10.6 = \mathbf{+4.4\text{ meals}}
\]
Conclusion: Of the \(7.5\) extra meals purchased, \(+3.1\) meals come from substituting toward cheaper food and \(+4.4\) meals come from higher real purchasing power.






NoteOptional Advanced Section: Lagrangian Optimization and the Slutsky Equation



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: Maximizing \(U(X, Y)\) subject to \(P_x X + P_y Y = I\) forms the Lagrangian \(\mathcal{L} = U(X, Y) + \lambda(I - P_x X - P_y Y)\). First-order conditions yield \(\frac{\partial U/\partial X}{P_x} = \frac{\partial U/\partial Y}{P_y} = \lambda\), where \(\lambda\) is the marginal utility of income. The Slutsky Equation decomposes total price sensitivity into compensated substitution and income terms:
\[
\frac{\partial X}{\partial P_x} = \underbrace{\frac{\partial X^h}{\partial P_x}}_{\text{Substitution } (<0)} - \underbrace{X \frac{\partial X}{\partial I}}_{\text{Income Effect}}
\]

title: 12  Chapter 12: Factor Markets, Labor Demand, and Wage Determination
text:
1. Conceptual Introduction
Up to this point, we have studied product markets, where households buy finished goods from businesses. Now we flip the Circular Flow diagram around to examine factor markets, where businesses hire the four inputs of production—labor, land, capital, and entrepreneurship—from households. Unlike pizza or concert tickets, firms do not hire workers for the personal enjoyment of watching people work; a company hires software engineers, nurses, or baristas solely because customers want to buy the goods and services those workers produce. Economists therefore call factor demand a derived demand—it is derived directly from consumer demand in the output market.
How does a profit-maximizing firm decide exactly how many workers to hire? It applies the exact same marginal principle we learned in Chapter 1, comparing the extra dollar revenue generated by hiring one additional worker against the extra dollar wage paid to that worker:

Marginal Revenue Product of Labor (\(MRP_L\)): The additional total revenue a firm earns by hiring one more unit of labor. For a firm selling output in a competitive product market at price \(P\), \(MRP_L\) equals the worker’s physical output contribution (Marginal Product of Labor, \(MP_L\)) multiplied by the selling price of the product: \(MRP_L = MP_L \times P\).
Marginal Factor Cost (\(MFC_L\)): The additional total cost incurred by hiring one more worker. In a competitive labor market where the firm is a wage taker, \(MFC_L\) simply equals the market wage rate \(W\).

Because diminishing marginal product causes \(MP_L\) to decline as more workers are added to fixed capital, the firm’s \(MRP_L\) curve slopes downward—and serves directly as the firm’s labor demand curve. A competitive firm hires workers up to the exact point where \(MRP_L = W\).


2. Visual Representation
Figure 1 shows a competitive firm’s downward-sloping Marginal Revenue Product of Labor (\(MRP_L\)) curve intersecting the horizontal market wage line \(W^*\) at the optimal employment level \(L^*\).



Figure 1. Competitive Labor Demand (\(MRP_L\)). A wage-taking firm hires workers until the value of the last worker’s marginal output (\(MRP_L\)) equals the market wage (\(W^*\)). Any shift in output price \(P\) or worker productivity \(MP_L\) shifts the entire \(MRP_L\) curve.




3. Real-World Application: AI Productivity Tools and Software Engineer Demand
When generative AI coding assistants boost a software engineer’s physical productivity (\(MP_L \uparrow\)) or when surging enterprise demand raises cloud software prices (\(P \uparrow\)), each engineer’s Marginal Revenue Product (\(MRP_L = MP_L \times P\)) shifts rightward—raising the equilibrium market wage and expanding hiring for skilled engineers. Conversely, if automated self-checkout kiosks substitute for routine cashier tasks, demand for manual cashier labor shifts leftward.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
For a competitive firm selling output at price \(P\) and hiring labor at market wage \(W\):
\[
MRP_L = MP_L \times P, \qquad \text{Hiring Rule: } MRP_L = W
\]
Worked Problem: A specialty coffee roaster sells bags of roasted beans in a competitive market for \(P = \$15\) per bag and hires packaging technicians at a daily wage of \(W = \$180\) per worker. The roaster’s daily output schedule is:

\(L = 1 \implies Q = 20\) bags
\(L = 2 \implies Q = 38\) bags
\(L = 3 \implies Q = 52\) bags
\(L = 4 \implies Q = 62\) bags
\(L = 5 \implies Q = 68\) bags

Compute \(MP_L\) and \(MRP_L\) for each worker and determine the profit-maximizing number of technicians to hire.
Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Compute \(MP_L = \Delta Q / \Delta L\) and \(MRP_L = MP_L \times \$15\) for Each Worker:
Worker 1: \(MP_1 = 20 - 0 = 20\text{ bags} \implies MRP_1 = 20 \times \$15 = \mathbf{\$300}\)
Worker 2: \(MP_2 = 38 - 20 = 18\text{ bags} \implies MRP_2 = 18 \times \$15 = \mathbf{\$270}\)
Worker 3: \(MP_3 = 52 - 38 = 14\text{ bags} \implies MRP_3 = 14 \times \$15 = \mathbf{\$210}\)
Worker 4: \(MP_4 = 62 - 52 = 10\text{ bags} \implies MRP_4 = 10 \times \$15 = \mathbf{\$150}\)
Worker 5: \(MP_5 = 68 - 62 = 6\text{ bags} \implies MRP_5 = 6 \times \$15 = \mathbf{\$90}\)
Compare \(MRP_L\) to the Daily Wage (\(W = \$180\)):
Workers 1, 2, and 3 generate \(\$300\), \(\$270\), and \(\$210\) in extra revenue—each exceeding their \(\$180\) daily wage.
Worker 4 generates only \(\$150 < \$180\), which would reduce profit by \(\$30\).

Conclusion: The roaster should hire \(L^* = 3\) technicians, earning a net surplus above wages of \((\$300 - \$180) + (\$270 - \$180) + (\$210 - \$180) = \$240\).

title: 12  Chapter 12: Factor Markets, Labor Demand, and Wage Determination
section: 12.2 Labor Supply and Competitive Market Equilibrium
text:
12.2 Labor Supply and Competitive Market Equilibrium

1. Conceptual Introduction
While firms form the demand side of the labor market, individual workers form the labor supply side. Every worker faces a fundamental trade-off between paid work (which generates income to buy consumption goods) and leisure (time spent resting, studying, or caring for family). The opportunity cost of an hour of leisure is the hourly wage \(W\) you give up by not working.
When the market wage rises, two competing behavioral effects tug on a worker’s hours:

The Substitution Effect: A higher wage makes leisure more expensive in terms of foregone earnings, motivating the worker to substitute away from leisure and work more hours.
The Income Effect: A higher wage makes the worker wealthier; because leisure is a normal good, higher income encourages the worker to “buy” more leisure and work fewer hours.

Across an entire occupation or industry, higher wages attract new workers from other sectors, so the market labor supply curve slopes upward. Equilibrium wage \(W^*\) and employment \(L^*\) settle where market labor supply equals market labor demand.


2. Visual Representation
Figure 2 shows how an increase in labor demand (from \(D_{L1}\) to \(D_{L2}\)) raises both equilibrium wages and employment in a competitive occupation.



Figure 2. Competitive Labor Market Equilibrium. Rising productivity or higher product demand shifts labor demand rightward from \(D_{L1}\) to \(D_{L2}\), raising equilibrium wages from \(W_1^*\) to \(W_2^*\) and expanding employment from \(L_1^*\) to \(L_2^*\).




3. Real-World Application: Nursing Shortages and Demographic Shifts
As the U.S. population ages, demand for hospital and outpatient healthcare services has surged—shifting the derived demand for registered nurses (\(D_L\)) sharply rightward. Because becoming a licensed nurse requires years of clinical training, short-run nursing supply is relatively steep, driving substantial wage increases and sign-on bonuses across metropolitan hospital systems.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Market labor equilibrium solves \(L_d(W^*) = L_s(W^*)\):
\[
W_d(L^*) = W_s(L^*)
\]
Worked Problem: In a metropolitan market for certified electricians, labor demand is \(L_d = 1{,}200 - 15W\) and labor supply is \(L_s = 200 + 10W\) (where \(W\) is the hourly wage in dollars and \(L\) is the number of employed electricians). Find the equilibrium wage \(W^*\) and equilibrium employment \(L^*\).
Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Set Labor Demand Equal to Labor Supply (\(L_d = L_s\)):

\[
1{,}200 - 15W^* = 200 + 10W^*
\]

Solve for Equilibrium Hourly Wage (\(W^*\)):

\[
1{,}000 = 25W^* \implies W^* = \mathbf{\$40\text{ per hour}}
\]

Substitute \(W^* = \$40\) to Find Equilibrium Employment (\(L^*\)):

\[
L^* = 200 + 10(40) = 200 + 400 = \mathbf{600\text{ electricians}}
\]
Conclusion: The competitive labor market clears at a wage of \(\$40\) per hour with \(600\) electricians employed.

title: 12  Chapter 12: Factor Markets, Labor Demand, and Wage Determination
section: 12.3 Monopsony Power and Minimum Wage Floors
text:
12.3 Monopsony Power and Minimum Wage Floors

1. Conceptual Introduction
What happens when a single dominant employer—such as a rural hospital system, a remote mining company, or a dominant regional warehouse hub—is the primary buyer of labor in a local town? Economists call a market with a single buyer (or dominant employer) a monopsony.
Unlike a competitive wage-taking firm, a monopsonist faces the entire upward-sloping local labor supply curve \(W(L)\). To attract one additional worker, the monopsonist must offer a higher wage—and because workplace fairness and payroll rules require paying the new higher wage to all existing employees as well, the Marginal Factor Cost of Labor (\(MFC_L\)) lies strictly above the labor supply curve (\(MFC_L > W\)).
To maximize profit, the monopsonist hires workers up to where \(MRP_L = MFC_L\), restricting hiring below the competitive level (\(L_M < L_C\)) and paying a depressed wage read off the labor supply curve (\(W_M < MRP_L\)). This creates a remarkable policy contrast:

In a competitive labor market, a binding minimum wage set above \(W_C\) reduces quantity of labor demanded and creates unemployment.
In a monopsony labor market, a carefully set minimum wage flattens the firm’s \(MFC_L\) curve over the lower range, which can increase both wages and employment simultaneously up to the competitive level!



2. Visual Representation
Figure 3 illustrates how a monopsonist equates \(MRP_L = MFC_L\) to restrict employment to \(L_M\) and depress wages to \(W_M\), below the competitive equilibrium \((L_C, W_C)\).



Figure 3. Monopsony Labor Market Power. Facing an upward-sloping labor supply curve, the monopsonist’s Marginal Factor Cost (\(MFC_L\)) rises twice as fast as the wage. Hiring where \(MRP_L = MFC_L\) restricts employment to \(L_M < L_C\) and depresses wages to \(W_M < W_C\), creating deadweight loss (orange triangle).




3. Real-World Application: Empirical Minimum Wage Studies in Local Labor Markets
Classic empirical research by economists David Card and Alan Krueger (and subsequent studies of regional hospital and retail labor markets) found that modest minimum wage increases frequently had little or no negative effect on employment—and occasionally increased employment—consistent with employers possessing local monopsony power due to worker commuting costs and search frictions.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
When inverse labor supply is linear, \(W(L) = a + bL\), Total Labor Cost is \(TLC = W(L) \cdot L = aL + bL^2\), and Marginal Factor Cost has twice the slope of labor supply:
\[
MFC_L = a + 2bL
\]
Worked Problem: A rural distribution center is a monopsonist facing an inverse labor supply curve \(W = 12 + L\) and Marginal Factor Cost \(MFC_L = 12 + 2L\) (where \(W\) is hourly wage in dollars and \(L\) is workers in tens). Its Marginal Revenue Product of Labor is \(MRP_L = 48 - L\).

Find the monopsonist’s profit-maximizing employment \(L_M\) and hourly wage \(W_M\).
Compare this to the competitive benchmark \((L_C, W_C)\) where \(MRP_L = W\).

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Solve for Monopsony Employment (\(L_M\)) and Wage (\(W_M\)): Set \(MRP_L = MFC_L\):

\[
48 - L_M = 12 + 2L_M \implies 36 = 3L_M \implies L_M = \mathbf{12\ (120\text{ workers})}
\]
Read the wage off the labor supply curve \(W = 12 + L_M\):
\[
W_M = 12 + 12 = \mathbf{\$24\text{ per hour}}
\]

Solve for Competitive Benchmark (\(L_C, W_C\)): Set \(MRP_L = W\):

\[
48 - L_C = 12 + L_C \implies 36 = 2L_C \implies L_C = \mathbf{18\ (180\text{ workers})}
\]
\[
W_C = 12 + 18 = \mathbf{\$30\text{ per hour}}
\]
Conclusion: Monopsony power cuts hiring from \(180\) down to \(120\) workers and depresses wages from \(\$30\) to \(\$24\) per hour. Setting a minimum wage at \(\$28\) or \(\$30\) per hour would raise both wages and employment.






NoteOptional Advanced Section: Calculus of Monopsony Optimization



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: Let revenue be \(R(L)\) with \(MRP_L = R'(L)\), and inverse labor supply be \(W(L)\) with \(W'(L) > 0\). The monopsonist maximizes \(\pi(L) = R(L) - W(L) \cdot L\). Differentiating with respect to \(L\):
\[
\frac{d\pi}{dL} = R'(L) - \left[ W(L) + L \cdot W'(L) \right] = 0 \implies MRP_L = W(L) \left( 1 + \frac{1}{\varepsilon_{L,s}} \right) = MFC_L
\]
where \(\varepsilon_{L,s} = \frac{dL}{dW}\frac{W}{L}\) is the wage elasticity of labor supply. The less elastic the local labor supply, the wider the markdown between \(MRP_L\) and the wage paid.

title: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design
text:
1. Conceptual Introduction
Standard supply-and-demand models assume that buyers and sellers share the exact same information about product quality. In many real-world markets—used cars, health insurance, bank loans, and job hiring—one side possesses private knowledge that the other side cannot observe. Economists call this imbalance asymmetric information, and it produces two distinct market failures depending on when the hidden information occurs:

Adverse Selection (Hidden Characteristics Before a Contract): When sellers or applicants know their private quality or risk type before signing a contract, uninformed buyers offer a single pooled price based on average expected quality. High-quality sellers (or healthy insurance applicants) find that pooled price unattractive and exit the market—lowering average quality further and causing the market to unravel (George Akerlof’s classic “Market for Lemons”).
Signaling and Screening: Markets counter adverse selection using two mechanisms. Signaling occurs when the informed party takes a costly, credible action to reveal high quality (e.g., a used-car dealer offering a 3-year powertrain warranty, or a job applicant earning a rigorous college degree). Screening occurs when the uninformed party designs a menu of choices to separate hidden types (e.g., an auto insurer offering high-deductible vs. low-deductible plans).



2. Visual Representation
Figure 1 illustrates adverse selection in a health insurance risk pool: when insurers charge a single pooled premium based on average risk, low-risk enrollees drop out, driving average medical costs and premiums steadily upward.



Figure 1. Adverse Selection and Risk-Pool Unraveling. At a single pooled break-even premium \(P_{\text{pool}}\), low-risk individuals on the right have willingness to pay below the pooled price and drop out, pushing average pool costs upward.




3. Real-World Application: Certified Pre-Owned Vehicle Programs
Private used-car markets suffer heavily from adverse selection because owners of reliable vehicles refuse to sell at discounted “average” prices. Automakers solve this information gap through Certified Pre-Owned (CPO) inspections and extended factory warranties—a credible signal that would be prohibitively expensive to honor on a defective car.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Under pooled pricing with asymmetric information, uninformed buyers offer the expected value across remaining types:
\[
E[V] = p_H V_H + p_L V_L
\]
Worked Problem: In a used-car market, \(50\%\) of cars are high-quality (“peaches”) worth \(\$12{,}000\) to buyers (and \(\$10{,}500\) to sellers), and \(50\%\) are low-quality (“lemons”) worth \(\$6{,}000\) to buyers (and \(\$5{,}000\) to sellers). Buyers cannot tell peaches from lemons before purchase.

Compute the maximum pooled price uninformed buyers are willing to pay if all cars are offered for sale.
Determine which cars actually get sold and what the final equilibrium price becomes.

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Compute Initial Pooled Willingness to Pay (\(E[V]\)):

\[
E[V] = 0.50(\$12{,}000) + 0.50(\$6{,}000) = \$6{,}000 + \$3{,}000 = \mathbf{\$9{,}000}
\]

Compare Pooled Offer (\(\$9{,}000\)) Against Seller Reservation Values:
Peach owners value their cars at \(\$10{,}500 > \$9{,}000\), so all peach owners withdraw from the market.
Lemon owners value their cars at \(\$5{,}000 < \$9{,}000\), so only lemons remain.
Update Buyer Beliefs (\(100\%\) Lemons Remaining): Knowing only lemons remain in the pool, buyers revise their offer downward to \(\$6{,}000\).

Conclusion: Asymmetric information drives every high-quality vehicle out of the market, collapsing trade to lemons only at \(\$6{,}000\).

title: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design
section: 13.2 Moral Hazard and Incentive Design
text:
13.2 Moral Hazard and Incentive Design

1. Conceptual Introduction
While adverse selection occurs before a contract is signed, moral hazard occurs after a transaction when one party’s hidden actions cannot be fully monitored by the other party. Whenever an insurance policy, corporate bailout, or fixed salary shields a person from the full financial consequences of their choices, they face weaker incentives to take costly precautions.
For example, a driver with zero-deductible comprehensive auto insurance may park in riskier neighborhoods or drive slightly less cautiously than an uninsured driver, and a homeowner with full flood insurance may build in a coastal floodplain. Moral hazard is not necessarily malicious fraud—it is a predictable behavioral response to altered marginal incentives.
To mitigate moral hazard while still providing valuable financial protection, insurers and employers design incentive-compatible contracts using three tools: (1) deductibles (requiring the insured to pay the first \(\$500\) or \(\$1{,}000\) of any claim), (2) co-payments and coinsurance (sharing a percentage of ongoing medical or repair bills), and (3) performance-linked compensation (aligning worker effort with firm outcomes).


2. Visual Representation
Figure 2 illustrates moral hazard in healthcare utilization: full insurance lowers the patient’s out-of-pocket price from \(P_0\) to \(\$0\), expanding doctor visits from \(Q^*\) to \(Q_{\text{insured}}\) where marginal medical benefit falls below the true resource cost \(MC\).



Figure 2. Moral Hazard in Health Insurance. Lowering out-of-pocket price from true resource cost \(MC\) to a low co-payment \(P_{\text{copay}}\) expands care consumption from \(Q^*\) to \(Q_{\text{ins}}\), generating overutilization where \(MC > MB\) (orange triangle).




3. Real-World Application: Deductibles in Auto Insurance and Coinsurance in Health Plans
Auto insurers rarely sell zero-deductible collision policies because even a small \(\$500\) or \(\$1{,}000\) deductible forces drivers to keep “skin in the game”—preserving strong incentives to drive carefully and avoid minor fender-benders while still protecting families against catastrophic \(\$30{,}000\) accidents.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
With a deductible \(D\) and coinsurance rate \(c\) (share paid by the insured above the deductible), a policyholder’s out-of-pocket cost on a loss \(L > D\) is:
\[
\text{Out-of-Pocket Payment} = D + c(L - D)
\]
Worked Problem: A homeowner chooses between two property insurance policies against a potential \(\$10{,}000\) storm damage claim:

Plan A: \(\$1{,}000\) deductible plus \(20\%\) coinsurance above the deductible.
Plan B: \(\$2{,}500\) deductible with \(0\%\) coinsurance above the deductible.

Calculate the homeowner’s total out-of-pocket payment and the insurer’s payout under each plan if a \(\$10{,}000\) loss occurs.
Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Evaluate Plan A (\(D = \$1{,}000\), \(c = 0.20\)):

\[
\text{Out-of-Pocket}_A = \$1{,}000 + 0.20(\$10{,}000 - \$1{,}000) = \$1{,}000 + \$1{,}800 = \mathbf{\$2{,}800}
\]
\[
\text{Insurer Payout}_A = \$10{,}000 - \$2{,}800 = \mathbf{\$7{,}200}
\]

Evaluate Plan B (\(D = \$2{,}500\), \(c = 0.00\)):

\[
\text{Out-of-Pocket}_B = \$2{,}500 + 0 = \mathbf{\$2{,}500}, \qquad \text{Insurer Payout}_B = \$10{,}000 - \$2{,}500 = \mathbf{\$7{,}500}
\]
Conclusion: Both plans require the homeowner to absorb at least \(\$2{,}500\) of the loss, preserving strong incentives to maintain roof and drainage protection.

title: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design
section: 13.3 Expected Value, Risk Aversion, and Expected Utility
text:
13.3 Expected Value, Risk Aversion, and Expected Utility

1. Conceptual Introduction
Why are households willing to pay insurance premiums that exceed their average annual claim payouts? Because most people exhibit diminishing marginal utility of wealth: gaining an extra \(\$1{,}000\) when you are already comfortable adds less happiness than losing \(\$1{,}000\) when you are struggling to pay rent. Consequently, most individuals are risk averse—given two prospects with the exact same average dollar payoff, a risk-averse person strictly prefers a guaranteed certain outcome over a risky gamble.
To model decisions under uncertainty, economists distinguish two criteria:

Expected Value (\(E[W]\)): The probability-weighted average of dollar outcomes across all possible states of the world. A risk-neutral agent cares only about Expected Value.
Expected Utility (\(EU\)): The probability-weighted average of the utility generated by wealth in each state. A risk-averse agent has a concave utility function \(u(W)\) and maximizes Expected Utility.

The maximum extra dollar amount above expected loss that a risk-averse person is willing to pay to eliminate risk completely is called the risk premium.


2. Visual Representation
Figure 3 plots a concave utility-of-wealth curve \(u(W)\), showing why a gamble between low wealth \(W_1\) and high wealth \(W_2\) yields lower expected utility \(EU\) than receiving the expected wealth \(E[W]\) with certainty—creating a positive risk premium between \(CE\) and \(E[W]\).






NoteClear It Up: Why Insurance Companies Can Profit While Customers Benefit



An insurance company pools thousands of independent risks across many households, diversifying away randomness so its payout per customer is nearly certain. Because risk-averse households gain utility by trading an uncertain catastrophic loss for a predictable annual premium, insurance creates mutual gains from trade even when premiums include an administrative markup above expected loss!





Figure 3. Concave Utility and Risk Aversion. Because \(u(W)\) bends downward (diminishing marginal utility of wealth), the expected utility of a 50/50 gamble (\(EU\)) lies below the utility of certain expected wealth \(u(E[W])\). The gap \(E[W] - CE\) is the risk premium.




3. Real-World Application: Smartphone Protection Plans vs. Catastrophic Health Insurance
Economic theory predicts that households should insure against large, catastrophic wealth shocks (home fires, major hospitalization) where diminishing marginal utility creates huge risk premiums—while self-insuring small, affordable losses (such as \(\$150\) phone screen repairs) rather than paying steep retail warranty markups.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
For two wealth states \(W_1\) and \(W_2\) occurring with probabilities \(p_1\) and \(p_2\) (\(p_1 + p_2 = 1\)):
\[
E[W] = p_1 W_1 + p_2 W_2, \qquad EU = p_1 u(W_1) + p_2 u(W_2)
\]
Worked Problem: A graduate student has initial wealth \(W_0 = \$10{,}000\) and utility of wealth \(u(W) = \sqrt{W}\). During the academic year, there is a \(20\%\) probability (\(p = 0.20\)) that their laptop and equipment are stolen, causing a \(\$6{,}400\) loss (leaving \(W_1 = \$3{,}600\)), and an \(80\%\) probability (\(1 - p = 0.80\)) of no loss (\(W_2 = \$10{,}000\)).

Calculate the Expected Wealth \(E[W]\) and Expected Loss without insurance.
Calculate Expected Utility \(EU\) without insurance, and find the Certainty Equivalent wealth \(CE\) (where \(\sqrt{CE} = EU\)).
Determine the maximum insurance premium the student would be willing to pay for full coverage.

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Compute Expected Wealth (\(E[W]\)) and Expected Loss:

\[
\text{Expected Loss} = 0.20 \times \$6{,}400 = \mathbf{\$1{,}280}
\]
\[
E[W] = 0.20(\$3{,}600) + 0.80(\$10{,}000) = \$720 + \$8{,}000 = \mathbf{\$8{,}720}
\]

Compute Expected Utility (\(EU\)) and Certainty Equivalent (\(CE\)):

\[
EU = 0.20\sqrt{3{,}600} + 0.80\sqrt{10{,}000} = 0.20(60) + 0.80(100) = 12 + 80 = \mathbf{92\text{ utils}}
\]
Find the Certainty Equivalent \(CE\) yielding \(92\) utils:
\[
\sqrt{CE} = 92 \implies CE = 92^2 = \mathbf{\$8{,}464}
\]

Calculate Maximum Willingness to Pay for Full Insurance: The student is indifferent between facing the theft risk and paying up to \(\$10{,}000 - \$8{,}464 = \mathbf{\$1{,}536}\) for full coverage—consisting of the \(\$1{,}280\) actuarially fair expected loss plus a \(\mathbf{\$256}\) risk premium (\(E[W] - CE = \$8{,}720 - \$8{,}464\)).

Conclusion: Because the student is risk averse, they will gladly buy full coverage at any premium up to \(\$1{,}536\).






NoteOptional Advanced Section: Arrow-Pratt Measure of Risk Aversion



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: For a twice-differentiable utility function \(u(W)\) with \(u'(W) > 0\), risk aversion requires strict concavity (\(u''(W) < 0\)). Economists measure the curvature of utility using the Arrow-Pratt Coefficient of Absolute Risk Aversion:
\[
A(W) = -\frac{u''(W)}{u'(W)} > 0
\]
For \(u(W) = \sqrt{W} = W^{1/2}\), \(u'(W) = \frac{1}{2}W^{-1/2}\) and \(u''(W) = -\frac{1}{4}W^{-3/2}\), giving \(A(W) = \frac{1}{2W}\)—confirming decreasing absolute risk aversion as wealth grows.

title: 14  Chapter 14: International Trade, Comparative Advantage, and Protectionism
text:
1. Conceptual Introduction
In Chapter 2, we saw that specialization according to comparative advantage expands consumption beyond domestic production limits. Now we use supply, demand, and surplus analysis to pinpoint who wins and who loses inside a country when it opens its borders to international trade.
To determine whether a small open economy becomes an importer or an exporter of a specific good, compare its autarky (no-trade) domestic equilibrium price (\(P_d\)) against the prevailing world price (\(P_w\)):

Importing Country (\(P_w < P_d\)): Foreign producers have a comparative advantage and can supply the good cheaper than domestic firms. Under free trade, the domestic price drops to \(P_w\). Domestic consumers cheer—buying more at a lower price and capturing a massive expansion in Consumer Surplus (\(CS\)). Domestic producers hurt—cutting production and losing Producer Surplus (\(PS\)). However, the gain to consumers strictly exceeds the loss to domestic producers, creating a net gain in Total Social Surplus.
Exporting Country (\(P_w > P_d\)): Domestic producers have a comparative advantage and can sell abroad at a higher world price. Under free trade, the domestic price rises to \(P_w\). Domestic producers expand output and gain more Producer Surplus than domestic consumers lose in Consumer Surplus—once again increasing net Total Social Surplus.

This sharp distributional split explains why trade policy is always politically contentious: the gains from free trade are spread thinly across millions of consumers (e.g., saving \(\$30\) on a pair of shoes), whereas the losses are concentrated among specific domestic factories and workers who lobby intensely for protection.


2. Visual Representation
Figure 1 illustrates an importing market where the world price \(P_w\) lies below the autarky price \(P_d\), expanding total social surplus by the green shaded triangle.



Figure 1. Welfare Gains from Free Trade (Importing Case). When \(P_w = \$40 < P_d = \$60\), domestic production falls to \(10\) and domestic consumption rises to \(30\), generating \(20\) units of imports and a net gain in Total Social Surplus (green triangle).




3. Real-World Application: Global Apparel and Consumer Electronics Trade
When U.S. retailers import smartphones, laptops, and apparel from specialized global supply chains at lower world prices, American households save thousands of dollars per year on everyday goods—expanding Consumer Surplus across the entire economy, even as domestic apparel manufacturing employment contracts.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
At world price \(P_w < P_d\), import volume and net social surplus gain are:
\[
\text{Imports} = Q_d(P_w) - Q_s(P_w), \qquad \Delta TS_{\text{trade}} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{Imports} \times (P_d - P_w)
\]
Worked Problem: In a small country’s market for steel, domestic inverse demand is \(P_d = 100 - 2Q\) and domestic inverse supply is \(P_s = 20 + 2Q\).

Find the autarky equilibrium price \(P_d^*\) and quantity \(Q_d^*\).
Suppose the country opens to free trade at a world price of \(P_w = \$40\) per ton. Calculate domestic quantity supplied, domestic quantity demanded, import volume, and the net gain in Total Social Surplus (\(\Delta TS\)).

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Find Autarky Equilibrium (\(P_d^*, Q_d^*\)): Set demand equal to supply:

\[
100 - 2Q = 20 + 2Q \implies 80 = 4Q \implies Q_d^* = \mathbf{20\text{ tons}}, \qquad P_d^* = 100 - 2(20) = \mathbf{\$60}
\]

Find Quantities and Imports at \(P_w = \$40\):

\[
40 = 20 + 2Q_s \implies 2Q_s = 20 \implies Q_s = \mathbf{10\text{ tons produced domestically}}
\]
\[
40 = 100 - 2Q_d \implies 2Q_d = 60 \implies Q_d = \mathbf{30\text{ tons consumed domestically}}
\]
\[
\text{Imports} = Q_d - Q_s = 30 - 10 = \mathbf{20\text{ tons}}
\]

Calculate Net Social Surplus Gain (\(\Delta TS\)):

\[
\Delta TS = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{Imports} \times (P_d^* - P_w) = \frac{1}{2} \times 20 \times (\$60 - \$40) = 10 \times \$20 = \mathbf{+\$200}
\]
Conclusion: Opening to free trade generates \(20\) tons of steel imports and increases national social welfare by \(+\$200\).

section: 14.2 Tariffs, Import Quotas, and Deadweight Loss
text:
14.2 Tariffs, Import Quotas, and Deadweight Loss

1. Conceptual Introduction
To shield domestic industries from foreign competition, governments frequently impose trade barriers—most commonly a tariff (a per-unit tax levied on imported goods) or an import quota (a legal cap on the physical quantity of goods allowed into the country).
When a small country levies a per-unit tariff \(t\) on imports, the domestic market price rises from \(P_w\) to \(P_w + t\). This price hike triggers four distinct welfare transfers, traditionally labeled Areas \(A, B, C,\) and \(D\):

Consumer Surplus Shrinks by \(-(A + B + C + D)\): Domestic buyers pay a higher price and buy fewer units.
Producer Surplus Expands by \(+A\): Domestic producers expand output at the protected higher price—a direct transfer from domestic consumers to domestic firms.
Government Tariff Revenue Equals \(+C = t \times \text{Imports}_{\text{tariff}}\): Collected on every imported unit that still crosses the border.
Deadweight Loss Equals \(-(B + D)\): Area \(B\) represents production inefficiency (using high-cost domestic factories to produce units that could have been imported cheaply at \(P_w\)), while Area \(D\) represents consumption inefficiency (mutually beneficial trades blocked by the artificial price hike).

An import quota restricting imports to the exact same volume raises the domestic price to \(P_w + t\) and causes the exact same deadweight loss \((B + D)\)—except Area \(C\) goes to whoever holds the valuable import licenses (quota rents) rather than the domestic treasury!


2. Visual Representation
Figure 2 illustrates the four welfare regions (\(A, B, C, D\)) created when a tariff \(t = \$10\) raises the domestic price from \(P_w = \$40\) to \(P_w + t = \$50\).






NoteClear It Up: Why Tariffs Create Two Deadweight Loss Triangles (\(B + D\))



Unlike a domestic excise tax (which creates one Harberger triangle), a tariff creates two separate deadweight loss triangles: Triangle \(B\) wastes resources by expanding inefficient domestic production above \(P_w\), while Triangle \(D\) destroys consumer surplus by pricing buyers out of the market above \(P_w\).





Figure 2. Welfare Effects of an Import Tariff. A \(\$10\) tariff raises domestic price from \(\$40\) to \(\$50\), cutting imports from \(20\) to \(10\). Consumers lose \(A+B+C+D\), domestic producers gain \(A\), the government collects tariff revenue \(C\), and society suffers deadweight loss \(B+D\).




3. Real-World Application: Solar Panel and Steel Tariffs in Downstream Industries
When tariffs raise domestic steel or solar-panel prices by \(20\%\), domestic steel mills and panel assemblers gain Area \(A\), while downstream U.S. manufacturers—automakers, construction firms, and rooftop solar installers—face higher input costs, illustrating how protection for one sector imposes direct costs on consumers and downstream jobs.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Under a tariff \(t\) raising domestic price to \(P_t = P_w + t\):
\[
\text{Tariff Revenue } (C) = t \times (Q_{d2} - Q_{s2}), \qquad DWL = B + D = \frac{1}{2} t (Q_{s2} - Q_{s1}) + \frac{1}{2} t (Q_{d1} - Q_{d2})
\]
Worked Problem: Continuing our steel market (\(P_d = 100 - 2Q\), \(P_s = 20 + 2Q\), \(P_w = \$40\)), suppose the government imposes a tariff of \(t = \$10\) per ton, raising the domestic price to \(P_t = \$50\). Compute Areas \(A, B, C,\) and \(D\), total Consumer Surplus loss, and net Deadweight Loss.
Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Find Post-Tariff Domestic Supply (\(Q_{s2}\)) and Demand (\(Q_{d2}\)) at \(P_t = \$50\):

\[
50 = 20 + 2Q_{s2} \implies Q_{s2} = \mathbf{15\text{ tons}}, \qquad 50 = 100 - 2Q_{d2} \implies Q_{d2} = \mathbf{25\text{ tons}}
\]
Post-tariff imports shrink from \(20\) tons down to \(25 - 15 = \mathbf{10\text{ tons}}\).

Compute Producer Surplus Gain (Trapezoid \(A\)):

\[
\text{Area } A = \frac{Q_{s1} + Q_{s2}}{2} \times t = \frac{10 + 15}{2} \times \$10 = 12.5 \times \$10 = \mathbf{\$125}
\]

Compute Government Tariff Revenue (Rectangle \(C\)):

\[
\text{Area } C = t \times \text{Imports}_{\text{tariff}} = \$10 \times 10 = \mathbf{\$100}
\]

Compute Deadweight Loss Triangles (\(B\) and \(D\)):

\[
\text{Area } B = \frac{1}{2} \times (15 - 10) \times \$10 = \mathbf{\$25}, \qquad \text{Area } D = \frac{1}{2} \times (30 - 25) \times \$10 = \mathbf{\$25}
\]
\[
DWL = B + D = \$25 + \$25 = \mathbf{\$50}
\]

Verify Total Consumer Surplus Loss:

\[
\Delta CS = -(A + B + C + D) = -(\$125 + \$25 + \$100 + \$25) = \mathbf{-\$275}
\]
Conclusion: Domestic consumers lose \(\$275\) in surplus; \(\$125\) transfers to domestic steel producers, \(\$100\) goes to government tariff revenue, and \(\$50\) is permanently destroyed as deadweight loss.






NoteOptional Advanced Section: Optimal Tariff Argument for a Large Country



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: While a tariff always reduces national welfare for a small price-taking country (\(P_w\) fixed), a large country whose import demand affects world prices can improve its terms of trade if a small tariff pushes \(P_w\) downward by \(\Delta P_w\). Net welfare changes by \(\Delta W = (\Delta P_w \times M_t) - (B + D)\), which is positive only if foreign exporters absorb more of the tariff than domestic deadweight loss—and only assuming foreign governments do not retaliate with counter-tariffs.
